question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old woman with a history of insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus complicated by distal symmetric neuropathy, permanent atrial fibrillation on apixaban, stage-3 chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL), and remote coronary artery bypass grafting was brought to the emergency department by municipal EMS after being discovered at 06:45 lying on the kitchen floor by her spouse, who had heard a thud from an adjacent room; she was reportedly last seen well at 05:30 preparing coffee and had not complained of headache, chest pain, or dyspnea earlier that morning. Paramedics arrived eight minutes after the 911 call, found her breathing on her own with a patent airway, seated her upright against a wall, applied a rigid cervical collar as a precaution against an unwitnessed fall, and transferred her onto a padded stretcher without administering dextrose, benzodiazepines, opioids, antiemetics, paralytics, hyperosmolar agents, or intravenous fluids other than a 5 mL saline flush through a single 18-gauge catheter placed in the left antecubital fossa. Finger-stick glucose in the field was 138 mg/dL and an on-board cardiac monitor demonstrated irregularly irregular rhythm at 96–104 beats/min with no acute ST-segment changes. Oxygen at 4 L/min by nasal cannula was provided solely to maintain saturation above 96 %. The 12-minute transport was uneventful, and no additional medications were given so that the hospital team could evaluate her neurologic state unaltered. She rolled into our resuscitation bay at 07:14, clothing damp from spilled coffee but free of blood or vomitus, still verbally responsive though intermittently incoherent. Simultaneous with the initial in-house survey—performed before any drug, imaging contrast, or fluid bolus—vital signs were blood pressure 148/78 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 102 beats/min in atrial fibrillation, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min with adequate tidal excursion, oxygen saturation 97 % on the prehospital nasal cannula, and core temperature 36.6 °C measured rectally. Airway assessment revealed moist mucosa, intact dentition, midline uvula, and a brisk gag when a Yankauer catheter touched the posterior pharynx; cough remained strong and protective. Both pupils were 3 mm, round, and brisk to direct and consensual light. During a 30-second period of quiet observation her eyelids stayed closed without flutter; however, the moment her surname was spoken in a normal tone just above either ear, the lids lifted to approximately three-quarters aperture, her gaze tracked toward the speaker, and remained open for several seconds before drifting shut again when questioning ceased. Speech was fluent yet disordered: she correctly stated her first name but insisted the location was her kitchen and the year was “2029,” repeatedly asking if the staff wanted breakfast. She misidentified the examining clinician as her late brother, laughed inappropriately, and provided rambling answers to orientation questions, though articulation and grammar were intact. Cranial nerve testing showed symmetric facial movement, palate elevation in the midline, and tongue protrusion without deviation; extra-ocular movements were full and smooth. Baseline limb tone was mildly increased in the lower extremities, normal in the upper. When asked, she squeezed the examiner’s fingers bilaterally with equal strength, lifted both arms to shoulder level for five seconds, wiggled toes on command, and rolled her eyes upward upon request, all without hesitation. Motor strength was 5/5 throughout by Medical Research Council grading, and there was no pronator drift. Deep tendon reflexes were 2 + and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles; plantar stimulation yielded flexor responses bilaterally. Sensation to light touch was grossly intact in all dermatomes, though she reported “pins and needles” in both feet consistent with known neuropathy. An attempt at rapid finger-to-nose testing revealed slow yet accurate targeting; heel-to-shin was steady. No abnormal flexor or extensor posturing, myoclonus, or tremor was observed during the examination. Cardiovascular auscultation documented an irregularly irregular S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; distal pulses were 2 + with capillary refill under two seconds and warm extremities. Lungs were clear to auscultation with resonant percussion and equal breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender; bowel sounds were present. Pelvic stability was preserved to gentle compression, and rectal tone was intact on digital exam. Inspection of the scalp disclosed a 1.5 cm superficial abrasion over the left parietal region with minimal dried blood but no palpable step-off or crepitus. No long-bone deformities, rib tenderness, or spinal tenderness were noted. A focused bedside ultrasound revealed no pericardial effusion and no free intra-abdominal fluid. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on room air yielded pH 7.37, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, PaO₂ 90 mm Hg, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, and base excess –1 mEq/L. Rapid serum chemistry panel returned sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, calcium 8.6 mg/dL, and glucose 142 mg/dL; international normalized ratio was 2.1 reflecting therapeutic anticoagulation. A 12-lead ECG repeated on arrival remained unchanged from the field tracing. No analgesics, sedatives, antiepileptics, antihypertensives, osmotic agents, or intravenous fluids beyond the initial saline lock have been administered in the department, ensuring that the lid opening only when verbally addressed, the disoriented conversational speech, and the consistent ability to follow motor instructions represent her unaltered neurologic baseline at the moment of presentation. Neurosurgery and stroke neurology have been paged emergently; non-contrast head CT, CT angiography of the head and neck, and MRI brain with diffusion sequences are being expedited, while point-of-care troponin and complete blood count are pending, continuous cardiopulmonary monitoring has been initiated, and frequent neurologic checks have been ordered every fifteen minutes.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses on the initial examination.
- Eye opening: Her eyes stayed closed at rest but opened when her name was spoken. Opening to voice = E3.
- Verbal response: She conversed but misidentified the place and year. Confused conversation = V4.
- Motor response: She squeezed fingers, raised her arms, and wiggled her toes on request. Obeys commands = M6.
Total: E3 + V4 + M6 = 13.
Final answer: 13
